# [Homepage](../index.html)

The theoretical exercises described below are quite [difficult]{.orange}. At the [exam]{.blue}, you can expect a [simplified version]{.blue} of them; otherwise, they would represent a formidable challenge for most of you.

On the other hand, the data analyses are more or less aligned with what you may encounter in the final examination.

:::callout-tip
The vast majority of these exercises are taken from the textbooks @Salvan2020 and @Agresti2015, possibly with a few minor modifications. You can consult these textbooks if you need additional exercises.
:::

## Data analysis

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Basketball` dataset - Partial solution: [`Basketball.R`](../code/Basketball.R)

The `Basketball` dataset can be [downloaded here](../data/Basketball.dat) and shows the three-point shooting, by game, of Ray Allen of the Boston Celtics during the 2010 NBA (basketball) playoffs (e.g, he made $0$ of $4$ shots in game $1$). Commentators remarked that his shooting varied dramatically from game to game.

In the $i$th game, suppose that $S_i = m_i Y_i$ is the number three-points shots made out of $m_i$ attempts is distributed as $S_i \sim \text{Binomial}(m_i, \pi_i)$, and that the $S_i$ are independent. The original source of the dataset is the textbook:

> Agresti, A. (2015). *Foundations of Linear and Generalized Linear Models*. Wiley.

Import the data and then

(a) Fit the null model, with $\pi_i = \pi$. Find and interpret the estimate $\hat{\pi}$, obtain its standard error and a confidence interval.

(b) Is there evidence of overdispersion? Motivate your answer based on the data. 

(c) Describe a factor that could cause [overdispersion]{.blue}. Adjust the standard error for overdispersion and obtain another confidence interval based on this correction.

(d) Compare the two confidence intervals and interpret the results. 
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Bioassay` dataset - Partial solution: [`Bioassay.R`](../code/Bioassay.R)

The data in the `Bioassay` dataset, available in the `MLGdata` library, refer to a biological experiment. The variable `y` represents the number of observed events out of a total of subjects (`den`) exposed to a dose `z`. The original source of the data is

> Finney, D. J. (1947). *Probit Analysis*. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

Import the data and then:

(a) Fit a binomial model with a probit link function. 

(b) To check for possible overdispersion, consider a quasi-likelihood model. Compare its standard errors with those of the probit model.

(c) Compute the variance of the standardized Pearson residuals for the probit model and the quasi-likelihood model. Comment the results.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Germination` dataset (continuation)

Reconsider the `Germination` dataset previously analyzed in [Exercises C](exe_C.html).

Evaluate the possible presence of [overdispersion]{.orange} and, if needed, account for it using a [quasi-likelihood]{.blue} model. Compare the results with those of the binomial model, propose a [final model]{.blue} and interpret the results.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### `Heart` dataset (continuation)

Reconsider the `Heart` dataset previously analyzed in [Exercises C](exe_C.html).

Evaluate the possible presence of [overdispersion]{.orange} and, if needed, account for it using a [quasi-likelihood]{.blue} model. Compare the results with those of the binomial model, propose a [final model]{.blue} and interpret the results.
:::

## Theoretical

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise A

Does the inflated-variance quasi-likelihood approach make sense as a way to generalize the ordinary normal model with $v(\mu_i) = \sigma^2$? Why or why not?

:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise B

Altham (1978) introduced the discrete distribution
$$
f(x; \pi, \theta) = c(\pi, \theta) \binom{n}{x}\pi^x(1 - \pi)^{n - x}\theta^{x(n-x)}, \qquad x = 0, 1,\dots, n,
$$
where $c(\pi, \theta)$ is a normalizing constant. 

Show that this is in the two-parameter exponential family and that the binomial occurs when $\theta = 1$. 

[Comment]{.blue}: Altham noted that overdispersion occurs when $\theta < 1$. Lindsey and Altham (1998) used this as the basis of an alternative model to the beta-binomial.
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse=true}
#### Exercise C

Consider the quasi-likelihood model of Unit E, which only assumes $\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mu_i = g^{-1}(\bm{x}_i^T\beta)$, $\text{var}(Y_i) = (\phi/\omega_i) v(\mu_i)$, and independence. Let
$$
q_r(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(Y_i - \mu_i)}{\text{var}(Y_i)}\frac{\partial \mu_i}{\partial \beta_r}, \qquad r = 1,\dots,p,
$$
be the [quasi-score]{.blue} and let $\bm{q}(\beta) = (q_1(\beta), \dots, q_p(\beta))^T$.

(a) Show that $\mathbb{E}\{\bm{q}(\beta)\} = \bm{0}$.

(b) Show that $\mathbb{E}\{\bm{q}(\beta)\bm{q}(\beta)^T\} = \bm{X}^T\bm{W}\bm{X}$, where $\bm{W}$ are the GLM weights of Unit B, and that this matrix coincides with $-\mathbb{E}\{\partial \bm{q}(\beta)/\partial \beta^T\}$.

(c) Let $S_i = m_i Y_i = \sum_{j=1}^{m_i} Z_{ij}$, where $Z_{ij} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\mu_i)$ and any two trials of the same group have correlation $\rho > 0$. Show that
$$
\text{var}(Y_i) = \frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{m_i}\{1 + \rho(m_i - 1)\}.
$$
Is the variance inflation factor constant across observations? Comment on the use of a quasi-binomial model in this case.
:::
